title: The font at the door
hookLine: some churches put the font by the door: you enter by baptism

lines: A STONE BASIN BY THE DOOR.
cards: Rain on her coat, a woman comes in off the street. Two steps in, her hand goes out to a small stone basin fixed to the wall.
She dips her fingertips, touches her forehead, her chest, one shoulder, the other, and walks on without breaking stride. Behind her, a father lifts a small boy up so he can reach the water too.
In other churches, the big font itself, where people are baptized, stands just inside the entrance, so everyone who comes in walks past it. Water first. Then the rest of the church.

teach.h: BORN OF WATER AND OF THE SPIRIT.
teach.b: Some churches put the font at the door for one reason: in Christian teaching, a person enters the church by baptism. Start with the entrance.

In John's Gospel, Jesus tells Nicodemus, "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God." Enter is the word, so the water sits where you enter. Next, the meaning.

Paul describes baptism as a burial: "Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life."
Down into the water, up out of it, and then you walk.
With the font by the door, every walk up the aisle starts beside that water. Then, the door. Jesus says, "I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved."
A font beside the door puts the two pictures side by side. Last, the fingertips. Catholics dip their fingers in holy water on the way in and make the sign of the cross.
Some describe it as a reminder, every time, of their baptism. Not every church places its water at the entrance. Some baptize at the front, before the whole congregation, and some in a river.

As day one hundred fifty-two showed, Catholic, Orthodox and some other churches baptize infants; Baptists and some others baptize those old enough to speak their own faith. Different doors, the same water.

how: Catholics dip their fingers in holy water at the church door and make the sign of the cross as they enter; in some churches the baptismal font itself stands near the entrance, while others baptize at the front or in a river.

o: water at the entrance, since baptism is the way in
a water tank kept by the door in case of fire
a fountain where visitors leave coins for luck

games.q: you walk into a Catholic church behind a woman coming in from the rain. just inside the door is a small basin of water. what does she do?
o: dips her fingertips and makes the sign of the cross
games.why: fingertips in the water, then forehead, chest, shoulders: a small reminder of baptism, every time she comes in.

practice: Dip your fingertips in a little water, at a doorway if you can, and touch your forehead, letting it dry on its own.
If you pray, and it's your custom, make the sign of the cross, or say a line from Psalm 51: wash me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin.
Or simply stand in the doorway, feeling the water, before you step through.

wordCard.voice: The font at the door. Water at a church's entrance, because in Christian teaching a person enters by baptism, and passes it every time they come in.

orig.note: Greek: the verb the New Testament uses for baptizing.

carryVoice: Your line: enter by water. Every walk inside begins right beside it. See you tomorrow.
